items.title: Wall Street week ahead: Fed minutes, unemployment data, consumer sentiment update
items.summary: Wall Street has a busy week ahead with a mix of economic updates and details about the Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates at its last meeting. The updates include fresh data on the health of the services sector, unemployment and consumer sentiment. Those reports can help give investors and economists more insight into how businesses and households are adapting to persistently high inflation. The minutes from the Fed’s last meeting will also give Wall Street more details about the central bank’s decision-making process for interest rate policy.

items.title: What a hiring slowdown signals about the state of the U.S. economy
items.summary: U.S. hiring slowed in September as employers added just 29,000 jobs. The disappointing jobs report has wide-reaching implications for consumer prices and interest rates, and it comes a month before Americans head to the polls for midterm elections. Amna Nawaz discussed more with Beth Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland.

items.title: US stocks rise near their record after the latest jobs report eases worries about inflation
items.summary: U.S. stocks are rising near their record after the latest jobs report cooled worries that a potentially hot U.S economy could make inflation worse. The S&P 500 climbed 0.7% Friday and pulled within 1% of its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 233 points, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.2%. They got a boost after a report showed U.S. employers slowed their hiring last month. That pushed traders to pare bets that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates later this month. Treasury yields initially tumbled but later retraced their losses as oil prices recovered most of an early swoon.

items.title: U.S. hiring stalls at 29,000, yet Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq surge: Why Wall Street welcomed September’s weak jobs report
items.summary: US jobs report and markets: The U.S. added only 29,000 jobs in September, far below the 90,000 economists expected. Unemployment also edged up to 4.2%. On the surface, that looks like bad news for the economy. Wall Street saw another side of it. The Dow rose 0.64%, the S&P 500 gained 0.90%, and the Nasdaq climbed 1.39%. The reason was the growing possibility that weaker hiring could reduce pressure on the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates high.

items.title: Job growth cools in September -- sorely missing forecasts
items.summary: Employers hired at a steady pace in September, enough to keep the unemployment rate steady and the Federal Reserve’s focus squarely on inflation – meaning more interest-rate hikes are likely.

items.title: The economy is resilient: Why do many Americans feel differently? An expert explains
items.summary: Even as the Federal Reserve moves to raise interest rates for the first time in three years, many of the metrics that economists rely on to gauge the overall health of the economy—like jobs reports, the unemployment rate and the stock market—have looked relatively strong in recent months. Despite this, only about 24% of Americans rated the economy as "good" or "excellent" in a recent Pew Research Center survey.

items.title: Fed’s Jefferson urges patience on rates; Kashkari sees more hikes ahead
items.summary: Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson stated that he sees no immediate need for further interest rate adjustments. He emphasized that future decisions would depend on analyzing economic data trends and risks. Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari expressed uncertainty regarding the timing of the next rate hike amidst strong economic performance. Both officials acknowledged the ongoing challenges of managing inflation that exceeds the 2% target.
